editorial.headline: Child Day-Care Education: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 88907 covers early-childhood education through child day-care services, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 88907 covers early-childhood education for children from birth to six years old, with priority given to those from birth to four. It includes provision organised by government or by the community, and expressly includes child day-care centres as well as centres established in cooperation with foreign educational institutions. The activity is therefore defined by its educational purpose and its focus on the earliest years of a child’s development.

Founders may register at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That range does not dilute the core remit: the work remains education for the birth-to-six cohort, with the stated priority for children up to age four. A founder should read the scope as one centred on an early-years educational programme delivered through a child day-care setting. The record also recognises that this may be organised publicly or by the community, and that cooperation with a foreign educational institution can form part of the day-care model.

Nationally, the PMA status is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, the national position permits the foreign stake in this activity to reach full ownership. That conclusion applies alongside the stated availability across every listed business scale. It is a clear national opening for the defined educational activity: early-childhood education through child day-care provision, rather than a generic label detached from the children, age range and educational purpose set out in the record.

Bali requires an equally direct reading. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island on a permanent basis. This entry, however, is not blocked by that rule. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, placing it outside the Low and Medium-Low risk group caught by the moratorium. The practical conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this child day-care education activity in Bali today. Bali’s result is affirmative because the record places the activity at the relevant higher-risk classification, not because the national foreign-ownership ceiling is being assumed to override the provincial rule.
